prompt: The generator you run in this lesson plants every defect on purpose and writes down where it put each one. What does that make possible?
hint: Think about a question real work almost never lets you answer.

choices.text: Grading the student's own cleaning automatically, file by file
choices.why: Nothing grades what you run on your own machine. The record is for the lessons, which measure their own techniques against it.

choices.text: Keeping the files small enough for a laptop
choices.why: The files are small by choice, but recording the defects has nothing to do with their size.

choices.text: Measuring how many of the real defects a technique found
choices.why: Right. With the answer written down, a matcher or a rule gets a score, not just a count of what it flagged.

choices.text: Hiding personal data from real customers
choices.why: There are no real customers here at all; every person is invented.

prompt: Put these steps in the order the course takes them.
hint: You measure before you change anything.
items: Profile the table before touching it
Decide what to do about missing values
Judge outliers: typo, real event or fraud
Record every transformation so it can be repeated
trap: Putting the record last is not leaving it for the end: lesson 17 gathers the habit every earlier lesson already practised.

prompt: The schema `raw` holds every file with every column as text. Why not declare dates as `date` and money as `numeric` from the start?
hint: What does `R$ 94,50` do to a `numeric` column?

choices.text: Text columns take less space on disk
choices.why: They take more, if anything. Space is not the reason.

choices.text: A typed column would refuse or silently reinterpret values before anybody has looked at them
choices.why: Right. `R$ 94,50` stops a numeric load, and `14/03/2025` is read the way the server's date style says. Text keeps what arrived.

choices.text: PostgreSQL has no `date` type for CSV files
choices.why: It does; `\copy` loads into any column type. The trouble is what the values look like.

choices.text: pandas would read the columns as text anyway
choices.why: pandas guesses types, and lesson 10 shows how those guesses go wrong. The database half is a separate decision.

prompt: Why is a virtual machine the recommended path for the lab?
hint: Look at what the setup adds to the system.

choices.text: The setup changes the whole system, and a snapshot undoes it
choices.why: Right. A database server and system packages are system-wide changes, and a snapshot taken once the setup is done gives a clean start after any experiment.

choices.text: pandas only runs inside virtual machines
choices.why: pandas runs anywhere Python does.

choices.text: The data is too large for an ordinary computer
choices.why: The files the course cleans are under 7 MB.

choices.text: Only a virtual machine has Ubuntu's packages
choices.why: A computer that already runs Ubuntu 24.04 takes the same commands; that is the installed path.

prompt: `psql` answers `FATAL:  role "bia" does not exist`. Which step of the setup was skipped?
hint: The server answered, so it is running.

choices.text: Starting the server
choices.why: A server that is down cannot say anything; `psql` fails earlier, at the socket.

choices.text: Activating the virtual environment
choices.why: `psql` is not part of Python, and the venv changes nothing about who connects.

choices.text: `createuser`, so the server has no role for that login
choices.why: Right. The server knows only `postgres` until somebody asks it to create a role with your login name.

choices.text: Setting `PGDATABASE`
choices.why: That names the database. The refusal is about who you are, not where you are going.

prompt: Why do the files you generate match the course's byte for byte?
hint: How does the program draw its customers and orders?

choices.text: It downloads them from the course
choices.why: Nothing is downloaded; the program writes every file itself.

choices.text: Its random generators start from fixed seeds
choices.why: Right. The same seeds draw the same sequence on every run and every machine, so every number in the course is yours too.

choices.text: pandas sorts the rows before writing
choices.why: The generator uses nothing outside Python's own library, pandas included.

choices.text: Python draws the same numbers whatever the seed
choices.why: A different seed draws a different sequence. The seed is what makes the run repeatable.

prompt: The database is created with `--locale=C.UTF-8`. What does that keep the same from one machine to another?
hint: Think about `ORDER BY` on a text column.

choices.text: How dates are read
choices.why: That is `datestyle`, the next setting.

choices.text: Which time zone the server uses
choices.why: That is `timezone`.

choices.text: Which files may be written
choices.why: That is `chmod -R a-w`, on the files rather than the database.

choices.text: The order text sorts in
choices.why: Right. Without it the database takes the machine's language, and two machines can put the same rows in different orders.

prompt: `wc -l raw/orders.csv` printed 28552. The file has one header line and no line breaks inside fields. How many data rows does it hold?
hint: Lines, less the header.

prompt: The query `sum(total)` over delivered online orders returned R$ 2,502,874.70. Which of these make that number indefensible? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four reasons were listed, and none of them raises an error.

choices.text: Some order numbers appear twice
choices.why: Yes. Each repeated row adds its total a second time.

choices.text: Some totals were typed by hand
choices.why: Yes. A typed total can be wrong and still be a number.

choices.text: The query excluded cancelled and refunded orders
choices.why: That is the query doing what was asked: revenue from delivered orders.

choices.text: The shops' sales are in another file the query never read
choices.why: Yes, if the question is the company's revenue; this query only answers for the online channel.

choices.text: `numeric` rounds the cents
choices.why: `numeric` is exact. A float would round; this did not.

prompt: The website writes `2025-01-01T11:24:01Z`. What does the `Z` say?
hint: It is a time zone.

choices.text: The time is São Paulo local time
choices.why: That is what the app's timestamps are, and they carry no `Z`.

choices.text: The order had a zero discount
choices.why: The discount is its own column; the `Z` belongs to the timestamp.

choices.text: The seconds were rounded to zero
choices.why: The seconds are right there, `01`. The letter is not about precision.

choices.text: The time is in UTC
choices.why: Right. In São Paulo that order was placed three hours earlier on the clock, at 08:24.

prompt: Match each birth year, typed for a customer born in 1978, to what it is.
hint: Validity is about the shape; accuracy is about the world.

pairs.right: Invalid, and probably what was meant

prompt: Every two-digit birth year in `customers.csv` came from one source. Which?
hint: Look at the split by `signup_channel`.

choices.text: The shops
choices.why: The shops produce the 1900s, a different defect.

choices.text: The app
choices.why: Right: 103 of the 106. The app stores what was typed without padding it.

choices.text: The website
choices.why: The website had no two-digit years at all.

choices.text: The 2023 migration
choices.why: Three of them, not the bulk.

prompt: The average age of customers with a four-digit year was 59.3 with the 1900s included and 45.2 without them. By how many years did the placeholder raise it?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: A delivery form requires a distance in kilometres, and couriers type `999` when they do not know it. What are those 999s?
hint: A rule for the format would accept them.

choices.text: Invalid values that a rule checking the column's format would catch
choices.why: `999` is a well-formed number of kilometres; only knowing the domain gives it away.

choices.text: Correct values for very long trips
choices.why: A grocer delivering inside five cities makes no 999 km trips.

choices.text: Valid values that are false: a missing distance wearing a number
choices.why: Right. They pass every format check and would drag any average up, exactly like the 1900s.

choices.text: Duplicates of a real distance
choices.why: Uniqueness is about rows that repeat, not about a value that recurs.

prompt: The company's own couriers delivered 14,847 orders and 14,406 have a time. What percentage is complete? Give one decimal place.
A pickup order has no delivery time. Why is that not a completeness defect?
hint: Completeness counts what should be present.

choices.text: The shop forgot to start the timer when the customer arrived
choices.why: There is no timer for a pickup; nothing was forgotten.

choices.text: Rapidex does not report times
choices.why: True of Rapidex orders, which are deliveries. A pickup has no courier.

choices.text: Pickups are too few to affect the column's completeness
choices.why: They are 5,315 of 26,533 delivered orders, about a fifth, and the size would not change the answer anyway.

choices.text: No delivery happened, so no value should exist
choices.why: Right. The blank is the correct answer, and filling it would create the defect.

prompt: 280 of the 618 customers who signed up in a shop have no e-mail. For which of these uses does that matter?
hint: Completeness is measured against a purpose.

choices.text: A campaign sent by e-mail
choices.why: Right. Those 280 cannot be reached by it, and no cleaning will produce their addresses.

choices.text: Counting customers per city
choices.why: The e-mail plays no part in that count.

choices.text: Adding up online revenue for 2025
choices.why: Revenue comes from orders; the customer's address is irrelevant to it.

choices.text: Finding orders that appear twice
choices.why: Repeated orders are found by order number.

prompt: PostgreSQL's CSV loader reads an unquoted empty field as ___, which is why `count(email)` skips it.
hint: The SQL word for the absence of a value.

prompt: Two rows of the city column both show `São Paulo` and still group apart. What is the difference?
hint: The screen shows the same word; the bytes are not the same.

choices.text: One was typed in a different font
choices.why: Fonts belong to the screen; the text has none.

choices.text: One stores the accent as a separate character after the a
choices.why: Right. The app writes the tilde apart; lesson 6 normalises it.

choices.text: One has a space at the end
choices.why: That is a third São Paulo, with 25 rows; it shows a gap in the listing.

choices.text: One came from the 2023 migration that mangled accents in names
choices.why: The migration's rows look different on screen: `SÃ£o Paulo`.

prompt: `max(signed_up)` for the app returned `12/31/2024`, though the app signed people up all through 2025. Why?
hint: What does `max` compare when the column is text?

choices.text: The app stopped signing people up at the end of 2024
choices.why: It did not; the query cannot see that because of how it compares.

choices.text: PostgreSQL reads `12/31/2024` as a date and ignores the rest
choices.why: Nothing is read as a date in `raw`; every column is text.

choices.text: Text is compared character by character, so the month decides before the year is read
choices.why: Right. `12/31/2024` beats `12/05/2025` at the fourth character.

choices.text: `max` skips rows from 2025 because of the time zone
choices.why: These are dates without a time; no zone is involved.

prompt: `orders.csv` has 28,551 rows and 28,526 distinct order numbers. How many extra copies are there?
hint: Rows less distinct ids.

prompt: Which of these rules checks consistency between two files?
hint: It needs to read two tables at once.

choices.text: Every customer in the file has an e-mail address on record
choices.why: That is completeness, inside one file.

choices.text: A birth year has four digits
choices.why: That is validity, one column at a time.

choices.text: An order number appears once in the orders file
choices.why: That is uniqueness, inside one file.

choices.text: An order's total equals its lines, less the discount, plus the fee
choices.why: Right. The total is in `orders.csv` and the lines are in `order_items.csv`.

prompt: December has 45 orders with no known customer, against 13 to 26 in every other month. What explains the extra ones?
hint: Compare the newest sign-up in the customer file with the last order.

choices.text: Christmas orders are placed without an account
choices.why: Every online order carries a customer id; the id is there, the account is not.

choices.text: The CRM export was taken on the 10th, three weeks before the year ended
choices.why: Right. Anybody who signed up after the export and then bought has no account in the file.

choices.text: Customers asked to be erased before the holidays
choices.why: Erasures explain the steady orphans of every month, not a spike at the end.

choices.text: The app duplicated December's orders
choices.why: Duplicated orders still point at real customers.

prompt: Orphan orders appear at a steady rate from January to November. What does the CRM team say they are?
hint: Their customers were not new.

choices.text: Orders of accounts deleted at their owners' request
choices.why: Right. The order stays as a fiscal record and the person goes, as the LGPD allows.

choices.text: Orders placed by staff while testing the checkout pages
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests test orders.

choices.text: Orders the website lost and rebuilt
choices.why: The orders are intact; it is the accounts that are missing.

choices.text: Customers from a city the company stopped serving in 2025
choices.why: The company serves the same five cities all year.

prompt: On 5 January the CRM export is 26 days old. Which of the two timeliness numbers is that?
hint: One is about an event; the other is about the moment you use the file.

choices.text: Latency
choices.why: Latency is the delay between an event and the data showing it.

choices.text: Completeness
choices.why: Completeness is about what is missing, not when the file was taken.

choices.text: Age
choices.why: Right. Age is how old the newest record is when you use it.

choices.text: Freshness ratio
choices.why: No such measure was defined here.

prompt: Why does the scorecard keep six separate percentages instead of one averaged quality score?
hint: Imagine the score drops next month.

choices.text: SQL cannot average percentages
choices.why: `avg()` would do it in one line; the objection is to the meaning.

choices.text: An average puts unlike defects on one scale and hides which rule moved
choices.why: Right. 25 duplicated orders and 348 false years are not the same kind of problem.

choices.text: The rules test different numbers of rows
choices.why: A weighted average would handle that, and would still hide which rule moved.

choices.text: Percentages above 10 are not reliable
choices.why: Nothing about size makes a percentage unreliable.

prompt: Put the steps from a quality dimension to a trend in order.
hint: A heading cannot be run; a rule can.
items: Name the dimension you care about
Write a rule a query can check
Count the rows tested and the rows failing
Run the same rule on next month's export
trap: Counting before the rule is written is the common slip: without a rule there is nothing to count.

prompt: Which of these are rules a query can check? Choose all that apply.
hint: Could you write a `WHERE` for it?

choices.text: Every customer has an e-mail address
choices.why: Yes: `email IS NULL` finds the failures.

choices.text: The data should be accurate
choices.why: A heading. Accurate in what way, measured how?

choices.text: An order number appears once
choices.why: Yes: compare `count(*)` with `count(DISTINCT order_id)`.

choices.text: Quality has to be high enough for the board
choices.why: An aim, not a rule.

choices.text: A birth year matches `^[0-9]{4}$`
choices.why: Yes, and the scorecard uses exactly this.

prompt: Next month the e-mail rule jumps from 11.7% failing to 40%. What should Ana do first?
hint: When a rule fails, split the failures by something.

choices.text: Fill the missing addresses with a placeholder so the rule passes
choices.why: That makes the rule lie; a placeholder is exactly the 1900 problem.

choices.text: Average the jump with the other five rules
choices.why: That hides it, which is the opposite of the point.

choices.text: Lower the threshold to 40% since the data has changed
choices.why: Moving the bar before knowing why the number moved explains nothing.

choices.text: Split the failures by signup channel to see which source changed
choices.why: Right. A jump like that is a form or an export that changed, and the split names it.

prompt: Match each rule from the scorecard to its dimension.
hint: One dimension on the right is not used.

pairs.left: A birth year has four digits
The order's customer is in the CRM
The CRM knows last week's buyers
